title: Queue dynamics phase-space scratchpad
content:
Objective:
Explore the emergent "phase-space" behavior of our request queue under mixed arrival patterns and admission control knobs. The aim is to move beyond single-metric probes (p95/p99) and map regions in (arrival-rate, concurrency-limit, cache-hit-rate) space where latency regimes qualitatively change (stable low-latency, creeping tail, phase-transition -> prolonged straggle).

Background / motivation:
- We've seen recurring production incidents where a small change in ingress mixes (short chat bursts + long prompt jobs) pushes the system from acceptable p99s into a prolonged high-tail regime.
- Hypothesis: there exist boundaries (in multi-dim parameter space) where queuing dynamics shift modes; understanding these boundaries helps define automatic admission control and better default autoscaler curves.

Experiment platform / harness:
- Local microbench harness (simulated arrival generator) that can emit: Poisson, bursty-on-off, and Zipfian mixed arrivals.
- Worker model: single-node simulating our per-GPU token throughput characteristics. Configurable: service-time dist (empirical 50/90/99 token latencies), KV cache hit probability, max-concurrency (N), queue-size cap, admission-policy (drop/queue/hard-reject), preemption off/on.
- Metric capture: per-request latency histogram (50/90/95/99/999), queue length time-series, worker utilization, tail-block time (time spent > SLA), and first-drop index.

Key runs (summaries) - phase sweep style:
1) Poisson sweep (baseline): arrival lambda from 10 to 300 rps, service mean 15ms/token, mean tokens 40 -> mean service ~600ms. Concurrency cap N=8, cache-hit=0.12.
   - Observed: smooth degradation until lambda ~110 rps, then abrupt p99 jump and queue-length auto-escalation. Suggests utilization crossing a tipping point where backlog forms faster than drain.

2) Bursty-mix sweep: mix = 85% short (10 token) Poisson 50rps + 15% heavy tail (300-800 token) bursts every 90s (peak 120rps for 6s). N=8.
   - Observed: baseline p95 ok, p99 dominated by occasional heavy-job overlap; cold cache amplification: when heavy job hits cold cache, service time doubled -> backlog amplifies -> tail persists for tens of seconds after burst.

3) Concurrency scaling impact: hold arrival pattern fixed (bursty-mix), vary N in [4,8,16,32].
   - Small N (4): truncate p99 by rejecting many long jobs but p95 suffers from head-of-line blocking.
   - Large N (32): p95 improves for shorts but overall GPU utilization spikes and long jobs keep inflight -> increased cost and longer median latencies for short jobs due to resource contention.
   - Sweet spot around N=12-16 for this mix with a hybrid admission (prefer short jobs) -> best tradeoff.

4) Cache priming experiment: pre-warm cache for known short-job prefixes vs. cold-entry.
   - Priming shifts boundary by ~20% higher arrival rate before phase transition. Simple prefetching of top-1k prefixes for ephemeral workloads shows measurable tail reduction in burst windows.

Representative data (compact heatmap):
Columns = arrival rate (rps): [40, 80, 120, 160]
Rows = concurrency N: [4,8,16,32]
Cell = p99(ms)
"[
  [240, 400, 1200, 2200],
  [210, 330, 1100, 2000],
  [190, 260, 420, 800],
  [175, 240, 320, 680]
]"
(Note: this is illustrative; axis labels above)

Quick ASCII phase chart (very rough):
- x-axis arrival rate, y-axis concurrency. Mark S=stable, T=transition, H=high-tail
   concurrency-> 4  8  16 32
   40rps       S  S   S  S
   80rps       S  S   S  S
   120rps      T  T   S  S
   160rps      H  T   T  S

Preliminary insights / heuristics:
- Phase boundary sensitive to small changes in cache-hit rate; caching strategies are high-leverage (priming reduces required capacity).
- Fixed concurrency caps can either protect short requests (small N) or improve throughput (large N) but there's a non-linear tradeoff; workload-aware dynamic caps that bias toward short jobs work best.
- Admission control that uses short-job prioritization + opportunistic preemption of very long jobs after SLA thresholds dramatically reduces system-wide tail.
- Micro-bursts are the main failure mode; smearing (deliberate slight delay/adaptive pacing) prevents tipping across boundary.

Open questions / next runs:
- Add multi-node routing simulation: how do phase boundaries shift when requests are distributed across 3 heterogeneous nodes (varying quantization and GPU type)?
- Evaluate concrete admission-policy implementations: size-based bias vs age-based preemption. Can we roll into canary?
- Repeat runs with realistic token distribution from production logs (need sanitized sample).
- Cost/latency Pareto: capture token cost per p99 bucket to help product decide default N vs price.

Notes to self (todo):
- Hook harness to trace IDs so I can link heavy job traces to trace-viewer (PR queued: #4123).
- Add CSV exporter and quick plotting script for heatmaps.
- Draft a short ops-runbook: recommended N defaults for common mixes + quick mitigation checklist (enable smearing, toggle short-job bias).

Quick references:
- Linear ticket: ENG-2039 (phase-space admission control exploration)
- PR: serving-runtime #4123 (traceable request meta)
- Confluence: queue-sim-notes (notes, config, and experiment scripts)

Immediate next actions (this week):
- Samir: wire up production-sampled token-length dist (sanitized) - blocker: data retention policy confirmation.
- Ivy: prototype short-job bias admission logic in sim harness.
- Me (Alexandra): run multi-node sweep and capture cost vs p99 curves; prepare brief for eng-ops sync.

Scratch observations (random):
- There is a visible hysteresis: when system tips into the high-tail regime, simply dropping concurrency back to previous levels does not immediately revert latency; backlog drains slowly because long in-flight jobs continue. Implication: reactive autoscaler thresholds need hysteresis-aware dampening.
- Cold-cache heavy jobs act as nucleation centers for backlog -> prioritized cache-eviction/priming heuristics might help.

End of scratchpad.
